bib.title: Survival Analysis and Censored Data (Chapter 11, An Introduction to Statistical Learning with Applications in Python)
bib.venue: Springer Nature Switzerland AG, Springer Texts in Statistics

question: How do we estimate survival curves, compare groups and regress on covariates when some outcomes are only known to exceed an observed censoring time?
contributions: Defines survival and censoring times, Kaplan-Meier, log-rank test, hazard function, Cox proportional hazards with partial likelihood, lasso/ridge-penalised Cox, C-index, time-dependent covariates, and a lifelines lab.

Dropping or ignoring censored patients biases survival estimates; independent censoring (T independent of C given features) is required and cannot be checked from the data.
results.quote: In general, we need to assume that the censoring mechanism is indepen-

limits: Only right censoring is treated; left and interval censoring are mentioned and not developed (p.471).
Independent censoring is assumed throughout and cannot be tested from data (p.471); non-informative censoring is called too technical.
Ties in failure times are ignored in the partial likelihood derivation; the tied case needs approximations (p.481).
Baseline hazard estimation, survival trees and random survival forests are only named, not worked (p.481, 488-489).
Cox model results are said to be fairly robust to violations of proportional hazards, but the check offered is only graphical (p.488).
The authors note survival analysis has received little attention in machine learning (p.470).
practices: Check how the status indicator is coded before analysis; the convention is 1 = event observed, 0 = censored (p.490).
Use the Kaplan-Meier estimator, not the proportion with Y>t, to estimate S(t) under censoring (p.472-473).
Use the log-rank test, not a two-sample t-test, to compare survival curves with censored data (p.474).
Fit a Cox model with all covariates rather than relying on a univariate log-rank test: confounding changed the Publication posres result from p=0.36 to highly significant (p.483).
Check proportional hazards by plotting log hazards per level, or stratifying a quantitative feature (p.488).
Do not use a fixed covariate for a state reached over time (Stanford heart transplant); use a time-dependent covariate (p.488).
Evaluate a Cox model on held-out data with risk-score strata or the C-index, because predicted survival times cannot be compared with censored true times (p.485-487).
Choose time zero deliberately (study end, birth, treatment date) because it changes what the model can measure (p.487-488).
Cross-validate the penalty lambda for Cox lasso on the partial likelihood deviance (p.485).

terms.definition: T is the time the event occurs; C is the time censoring occurs; we observe Y = min(T, C)
delta = 1 if T <= C, 0 if T > C
conditional on the features, the event time T is independent of the censoring time C
right: T >= Y; left: T <= Y; interval: event time known to lie in an interval
the patients alive and in the study just before death time d_k
S^(d_k) = product over j<=k of (r_j - q_j)/r_j; constant between death times
tests equality of two survival curves with W = sum(q1k - mu_k)/sqrt(sum Var(q1k)), mu_k = (r1k/rk) q_k; approximately N(0,1) for large samples
h(t) = lim Pr(t < T <= t + dt | T > t)/dt = f(t)/S(t); the death rate in the instant after t given survival to t
L_i = f(y_i) if uncensored, S(y_i) if censored; L = prod h(y_i)^delta_i S(y_i)
h(t|x_i) = h0(t) exp(sum x_ij beta_j) with h0 an unspecified baseline hazard
exp(sum x_ij beta_j), relative to the all-zero feature vector
PL(beta) = prod over uncensored i of exp(x_i beta)/sum over i' with y_i' >= y_i of exp(x_i' beta); h0 cancels
twice the cross-validated negative log partial likelihood; plays the role of CV error
C = sum over pairs y_i>y_i' of I(eta_i' > eta_i) delta_i' divided by sum over the same pairs of delta_i'
a predictor x_i(t) whose value changes over time; enters the partial likelihood as its current value at y_i
regression tree whose split criterion maximises the difference between survival curves in daughter nodes
